title: Cuban Revolution
summary: An armed and urban rebellion led by Fidel Castro's 26th of July Movement, begun with the failed Moncada Barracks attack of 1953, overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista on 1 January 1959 and went on to remake Cuba's state, economy and place in the Cold War.
card: Fidel Castro and about 165 followers attacked the Moncada Barracks in Santiago de Cuba on 26 July 1953; the raid failed, but its bloody aftermath and Castro's trial speech made the movement known. After the Granma landing of December 1956 and two years of guerrilla war and urban resistance, Batista left Cuba on 1 January 1959. The new government's trials and firing-squad executions, defended by Cuban officials and counted in the thousands by exile researchers, were the first of many contested measures.
what:
On 10 March 1952 General Fulgencio Batista seized power in a coup, ending Cuba's constitutional government. On 26 July 1953 a young lawyer, Fidel Castro, led about 165 men and two women in an attack on the Moncada Barracks in Santiago de Cuba, with side attacks on a hospital and the Palace of Justice. It was repulsed. By Castro's account most of the rebel dead were prisoners killed after the fighting. He was tried in September and October 1953, defended himself, set out a reform programme built on the 1940 constitution, and was sentenced to 15 years; a general amnesty freed him in the mid-1950s (MIT dates it to 1954).

The 26th of July Movement reorganised in Mexico and sailed to Cuba on the yacht Granma, landing on 2 December 1956, two days late. Batista's forces shattered the expedition, and a small remnant, counted variously as 12 to 17 men, regrouped in the Sierra Maestra. Over two years the rebels gained local and foreign support while an urban underground prepared sabotage and strikes. The United States suspended arms aid to Batista on 14 March 1958; the army's summer 1958 offensive against the Sierra failed; an opposition unity pact was signed in Venezuela in July 1958; and in December rebel columns took garrisons across Oriente and Las Villas and began the attack on Santa Clara on 27 December.

Batista left Cuba in the early hours of 1 January 1959, and on 2 January Castro named Manuel Urrutia provisional president. Special tribunals tried and shot Batista-era police and soldiers within days, and the legality, fairness and total number of these executions are still disputed. Within two years the government had expropriated US property, the United States had imposed an embargo (19 October 1960) and broken relations (3 January 1961), and Cuba had begun to become a one-party communist state.

uncertainty.note: The start is the Moncada attack (26 July 1953), from which the movement took its name; the 10 March 1952 coup is treated as a cause. The end is Batista's departure; the revolutionary government's transformation of 1959-1961 is covered in the text, not the span. Historians who date the revolution from the 1952 coup or the 1956 landing give a different start.

how: The sequence runs in five steps. (1) Batista's 1952 coup removed the constitutional order, which Castro later argued made the regime illegitimate and the 1940 constitution the only valid law. (2) The Moncada raid failed militarily; the army's killing of prisoners and the publicity of the trial gave Castro a national profile and a programme of land, wage, housing, education and health measures. (3) After exile in Mexico, the expedition landed on 2 December 1956 and was nearly destroyed, but a remnant regrouped in the Sierra Maestra and the movement gained growing local and foreign support, while an urban underground prepared strikes and sabotage. (4) Repression, the US suspension of arms aid on 14 March 1958, the failed summer 1958 offensive, the July 1958 opposition unity pact and defections eroded the army; US diplomats later judged that Batista left because he saw his position collapsing across Oriente, Camagüey and Las Villas. (5) Rebel columns overran garrisons in December 1958, began the attack on Santa Clara on 27 December, and Batista flew out on 1 January 1959.
why_it_matters: The revolution replaced a US-backed dictatorship with a government that, within two years, expropriated US property, saw the United States impose an embargo (19 October 1960) and break diplomatic relations (3 January 1961), and began on 16 April 1961 to convert Cuba into a one-party communist system. Inside Cuba, the new leaders announced a state campaign against racial discrimination in March 1959 after pressure from Afro-Cuban activists, although later scholarship finds it weakened by racist caricature in the media, the closing of independent Black institutions and the lack of Afro-Cubans in top posts. The 1959 trials began a pattern of state violence that the government and its critics still describe in opposite terms: its defenders cite justice for torturers and killers, while Cuba Archive documents thousands of firing-squad executions over the following decade. Later waves of emigration, including the 1980 Mariel exodus and the 1994 balsero crisis, are part of its legacy. Had the Moncada attackers been wiped out, or Castro killed in custody in 1953, or the small remnant of the 1956 expedition destroyed, the 26th of July Movement might have disappeared and other opposition groups could have shaped the post-Batista state, possibly without a break with Washington.

perspectives.holder: Fidel Castro and the 26th of July Movement (1953 speech); revolutionary press of 1959
perspectives.account: The Batista regime was illegitimate and the Moncada attack lawful resistance; most Moncada dead were prisoners murdered afterwards. In 1959 the newspaper Revolución defended the shootings of Batista-era torturers and killers as just and demanded by the public, citing about 550 military and police executed for the roughly 20,000 deaths attributed to Batista's last two years.

perspectives.holder: Cuba Archive (Maria C. Werlau) and Cuban exile historiography
perspectives.account: The executions began a campaign of terror that consolidated a communist regime. Cuba Archive documents 3,083 firing-squad executions since 1959, 2,737 of them in 1959-1969, and 8,172 deaths and disappearances in all to December 2024, and says the true total is higher.

The Santiago consul reported about 70 shot on 12 January, nearly 300 arrests, military boards made up mostly of rebel officers, most local lawyers declining to take part, and local approval of the executions alongside misgivings about process.

Racial discrimination was not an explicit plank of the 26th of July platform; Afro-Cuban activists pressed the new government, which announced an anti-discrimination campaign in March 1959, yet the campaign was weakened by racist caricature, the dismantling of independent Black institutions and under-representation of Afro-Cubans at the top.

numbers.note: Cuba Archive: 3,083 in all, of which 2,737 in 1959-1969 (the low figure is that subtotal). A non-governmental case-by-case count, presented in advocacy testimony.

numbers.note: Cuba Archive says the true number is many times higher; covers causes other than the 1959 executions.

audience_note: Covers the killing of prisoners after the Moncada attack, summary trials and firing-squad executions in 1959, and political repression before and after. No graphic images are included.

importance.justification: The revolution overthrew a US-backed dictatorship and created a one-party communist state in the Western Hemisphere that shaped Cold War politics from the Bay of Pigs onward.
